output.diagnosis: Use customer research first. With roughly 20 purchases per month, a conventional A/B test is unlikely to reach a reliable decision quickly unless the proposed change has a very large effect or traffic is accumulated over a long period. The lack of device breakdown also means you do not yet know whether a mobile, desktop, or channel-specific issue is driving conversion.
actions: Instrument and review the funnel before testing: sessions by device/channel, product-page views, add-to-cart rate, checkout starts, checkout completion, payment errors, page speed, and key landing pages.

Run qualitative research with recent purchasers and non-purchasers: short post-purchase survey, exit/abandonment survey, and 5–8 moderated usability sessions focused on finding a product, understanding suitability, ingredients/safety concerns, shipping/returns, and checkout friction.
Review customer-support tickets, reviews, returns, and social comments for repeated objections or confusion. Tag themes rather than relying on isolated anecdotes.

Use session recordings and heatmaps cautiously to generate hypotheses, especially for mobile navigation, product-page comprehension, variant selection, cart, and checkout. Do not treat recordings alone as proof of causation.

Prioritize low-risk, evidence-backed improvements that do not require an experiment to validate immediately, such as clarifying product benefits, routine/skin-type guidance, ingredient information, delivery/returns information, and checkout error messaging—provided research identifies these as issues.

After identifying a high-confidence hypothesis and obtaining device/channel data, run an A/B test only if you can define one primary metric, avoid major concurrent site changes, and are willing to run it until a pre-defined sample-size and duration requirement is met. If traffic remains low, use tests for major, well-supported changes rather than minor copy or design variations.
missing_information: Current conversion rate definition and whether the 20 purchases are unique orders.
Sessions and purchases by device, traffic source, landing page, country, and new versus returning visitor.
Funnel counts for product view, add to cart, checkout start, and purchase.
Top products, price points, subscription availability, shipping costs/timing, return policy, and payment methods.
Whether checkout is hosted or customizable, plus any known technical, payment, stock, or shipping issues.
Existing research sources: survey responses, reviews, support tickets, return reasons, analytics, and session recordings.
The specific conversion problem or proposed change you are considering.
caveats: Customer research identifies likely reasons and language to use; it does not quantify the conversion impact of a change.
A/B tests can still be useful at low volume, but inconclusive tests and long runtimes are common; do not declare a winner from early results.
Avoid changing many elements at once if you later want to learn which change caused an outcome.
Protect privacy and obtain appropriate consent when collecting survey responses or using behavior-recording tools.
